name: App Tracking Transparency
plain: A system prompt that asks whether the app may track the person across other companies' apps and sites.
meaning: Gates the IDFA and cross-company tracking; a No returns an all zero IDFA. Rules also forbid workarounds.

android.permission: AD_ID (normal, API 33); no per app prompt
android.prompt_ui: No prompt; user can delete the advertising ID in Settings
android.persistence: Global reset or deletion; zeros the ID
android.revocation: Settings > Privacy > Ads > Delete advertising ID
android.store_policy: Play: advertising ID policy; AD_ID declaration required for target 33
android.note: Apps targeting 33 without AD_ID get zeros

ios.prompt_ui: Allow or Ask App Not to Track
ios.persistence: Until changed; global switch Allow Apps to Request to Track
ios.store_policy: App Review 5.1.2(i): no tracking without ATT; no fingerprinting workaround
ios.note: Deny returns zero IDFA; industry reports opt in around 25 to 35 percent

limits.headline: Can track you across other companies' apps and sites only if you tap Allow
limits.user_action: You tap Allow or Ask App Not to Track on the system prompt
can: Use the iPhone ad ID once you tap Allow
Link your activity across other companies' apps and sites after you allow it
Use the ad ID on Android until you delete it in Settings (no prompt there)
cannot: Get the real ad ID after you tap Ask App Not to Track; it returns zeros
Work around your no with other tricks, which Apple's rules forbid
Show the tracking prompt on Android; there is none
Get the real ad ID on Android 13 apps that skip the AD_ID permission
limits.reach_label: Across apps, only if you allow it
limits.differs: iPhone asks with a system prompt (iOS 14.5 and later). Android has no prompt; you delete the ad ID in Settings.

story.what_it_is: The iOS pop up asking if an app may follow you across other companies' apps and sites.

marketing.name: App Tracking Transparency
marketing.pitch: Apps must ask for your permission before tracking you across other companies' apps and websites.

story.for_you: A pop up says 'Allow app to track your activity across other companies' apps and websites?' with 'Ask App Not to Track' and 'Allow'. You can also turn requests off in Settings.
story.for_makers: Saying yes unlocks the IDFA. A no returns zeros and forbids workarounds. Makers must design the ask well, show a pre prompt that explains benefits and plan ads around the lower yes rate.

use_cases.example: A free game explains that tracking keeps it free, then shows the ATT prompt.
A retailer shows a short screen about better offers before the pop up.
An ad network gets IDs for the opted in and falls back to SKAN for others.
A social app asks at launch, and sees yes rates near industry averages.
A news app delays the prompt until after a first article.
Apple can pull an app that tracks anyway.

story.android_note: Android uses a settings toggle for the advertising ID, not a pop up.
story.ios_note: Introduced in iOS 14.5. Regulators in Europe are challenging how it works.

technical_bounds: No consent means no IDFA; fingerprinting is barred
Probabilistic attribution still happens server side
Prompt only works while the app is active
Opt-in is roughly 25 to 38 percent depending on source (Adjust 38 percent Q1 2026; AppsFlyer 29 percent 2026 figure cited by trade press; gaming lower than non-gaming)
First-party data use is not 'tracking' under Apple's definition
Apple's definition covers linking with other companies' data for ads or measurement, or sharing with data brokers
Declaring tracking in the App Privacy label is separate
